analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the federal Department of Education by a set date.
analysis.headline: The one-sentence bill to abolish the Department of Education was referred to committee on the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 899 is a single sentence: the Department of Education would shut down on December 31, 2018. That department is the channel for nearly all federal support for schools and college students, including Pell Grants, federal student loans, and funding targeted to low-income school districts, and it enforces federal anti-discrimination rules in schools. Shutting it down would leave those programs without an administrator, and the bill proposed no replacement.
analysis.who_benefits: Very few ordinary people would benefit. The bill's supporters argue that returning education policy fully to states and local school boards would cut federal spending and federal red tape. The measurable savings would show up as slightly lower federal taxes, which accrue disproportionately to higher-income households. States would gain full control over education policy with no federal strings attached.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would eliminate the Department of Education entirely on December 31, 2018, eliminating the agency and its budget rather than reforming it [S2][S3].
It is a single sentence with no plan for what happens to the programs the department administers, reflecting an approach that treats the agency itself as the problem [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Low-income college students who rely on Pell Grants and federal loans would lose the office that administers that aid; school districts serving poor families would lose Title I money; students and families facing discrimination in schools would lose the federal office that handles those complaints. Roughly 4,000 federal employees would also lose their jobs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-income students and underfunded school districts

drawbacks.text: The department does not set curriculum or run schools; it primarily moves money and enforces civil rights law. Terminating it would cut off the pipeline for federal student aid and school funding without naming any successor agency, meaning Congress would either have to rebuild those functions elsewhere or abandon them [S3].
Termination on a fixed date with no transition plan would leave grants, loans, and civil rights complaints in limbo for the borrowers, districts, and families who depend on them [S3].

Even legislators who favor shrinking the federal education footprint generally pursue reform or block-granting rather than outright termination, because a hard shutdown strands commitments already made to students and schools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered no transition, no replacement agency, and no plan for the aid and funding programs it would strand. Whatever savings it promised were theoretical, while the losses to students and schools would have been immediate and concrete. As drafted, the costs clearly outweighed the benefits, which is likely why it drew only 13 supporters in the whole House.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for two years with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced the one-sentence bill on February 7, 2017, joined by 12 Republican cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1][S4][S5].
The bill text is a single line directing that the Department of Education terminate on December 31, 2018 [S3].

The complete action history shows only two entries: introduction and committee referral. No hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary students and schools, in effect: the programs the bill would have stranded, and the federal role in funding them, survived untouched. Nothing was gained, though, since the bill was symbolic and simply expired.

for.name: Rep. Thomas Massie
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to terminate the Department of Education and introduced it on February 7, 2017.

for.name: 12 of 238 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat joined.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 7, 2017 and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration in the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat supported the bill, but it never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call to measure broader support.

industries.industry: Private student lenders and loan servicers
industries.note: Ending the Department of Education would end the federal student loan program, pushing borrowing into the private market where loans are costlier and protections weaker. That is a business opportunity for private lenders, but a cost for students.

industries.industry: School districts and state education agencies
industries.note: Districts would lose federal formula funding for low-income students but gain freedom from federal requirements. The money is not replaced in the bill, so the net effect is a large unfunded change.
